1.quote: The income statement is represented by the simple formula: net income equals revenue minus expenses.
1.by: Dr. J, Answers with Dr. J
points: Net income = revenue minus expenses, the basic formula
The income statement covers three months, a year, or several years
Large companies add gains and losses to the same equation
It shows whether the business is profitable over the period

2.quote: Operating revenue refers to the revenue, the money that you earn from your bread and butter activities.
2.by: Dr. J, Answers with Dr. J
points: Operating revenue comes from your core activity
Non-operating revenue comes from secondary activities such as interest
Both appear on the income statement, but they are kept apart
Separating them shows how well the core business performs

3.quote: Gains are usually talking about the sale of a long-term asset.
3.by: Dr. J, Answers with Dr. J
points: A gain comes from selling a long-term asset
Non-operating revenue is recurring; a gain is a one-time event
A sale below book value is recorded as a loss
Losses appear at the bottom of the income statement

4.quote: Expenses fall in categories such as costs of goods sold, selling, general and administrative, depreciation or amortization, and research and development.
4.by: Dr. J, Answers with Dr. J
points: Cost of goods sold, SG&A, depreciation and R&D are the main categories
Payroll, commissions, rent and utilities are also expenses
The statement starts with revenue minus cost of goods sold
Clear categories make it easy to compare periods and competitors

5.quote: There's a single step income statement as well as a multiple-step income statement used by large corporations.
5.by: Dr. J, Answers with Dr. J
points: Single-step: one calculation from revenues to net income
Multiple-step: several intermediate results, used by large corporations
Large companies need it for mergers, acquisitions and regulators
Shareholders use it to judge management efficiency

6.quote: Income statements for your privately held company would not be public record. However, they do become public record when you want a type of certification.
6.by: Dr. J, Answers with Dr. J
points: Private company accounts are not public by default
Certifications and government contracts can make them public
Plan this before you set up a company for government work
Your financial information becomes visible to public scrutiny

7.quote: The balance sheet provides an overview of a company's assets, liabilities, and stockholders' equity at a point in time.
7.by: Dr. J, Answers with Dr. J
points: Assets = liabilities + owner's equity
The balance sheet is a snapshot at one point in time
Example: a $300,000 home with $250,000 owed leaves $50,000 of equity
If both sides do not match, something is recorded wrong

8.quote: The debt to equity ratio, which is simply dividing a company's total liabilities by its shareholders' equity.
8.by: Dr. J, Answers with Dr. J
points: Debt to equity = total liabilities divided by shareholders' equity
A high ratio means the company relies on borrowing
Investors use it to judge the financial risk they take
It is calculated from the balance sheet

9.quote: The quick ratio is an indicator of whether the company has sufficient short term assets to cover its short term liabilities.
9.by: Dr. J, Answers with Dr. J
points: The quick ratio checks whether you can pay your bills on time
It compares short-term assets with short-term liabilities
Profit on paper does not prevent a cash shortage
Investors and managers use it as a quick health check

10.quote: Companies like Google, Amazon, and Facebook didn't make any money their first years of operations, so they survived off other people's money.
10.by: Dr. J, Answers with Dr. J
points: Young companies can be financed by debt (bonds, notes) or equity
Many fast-growing companies lose money at the start
Outside money pays the bills until the business earns its own
Investors keep watching the ratios as the company grows

11.quote: Current assets can be converted to cash within one year or less.
11.by: Dr. J, Answers with Dr. J
points: Cash and cash equivalents: certificates of deposit, treasury bills
Marketable securities and accounts receivable (30 to 90 days)
Inventory you expect to sell within the year
Prepaid expenses such as a year of rent paid in advance

12.quote: Preferred stock does not represent ownership in the company. It simply represents a preference in the investor's investment when it comes to payout of dividends.
12.by: Dr. J, Answers with Dr. J
points: Common stock represents ownership in the company
Preferred stock gives priority when dividends are paid
Both sit in the shareholders' equity section
Retained earnings are the profits kept in the business

13.quote: The cash flow statement is broken down into three parts: operating, investing, and financing activities.
13.by: Dr. J, Answers with Dr. J
points: Operating: cash from the core business
Investing: purchases and sales of assets and investments
Financing: other people's money, such as shares and bonds
Together they show how well the company manages its cash

14.quote: Investing activities look at your investments: the actual cash needed to purchase a stock, before any interest it earns.
14.by: Dr. J, Answers with Dr. J
points: Operating activities: a detailed look at daily business
Investing activities: the cash spent on investments and equipment
Investing looks at the purchase itself, not only the income
Keeping them apart shows where the money really comes from

15.quote: The cash flow statement shows how well you are managing your cash and how effective you are at generating cash and paying your bills.
15.by: Dr. J, Answers with Dr. J
points: Operating activities relate to the income statement
Investing activities relate to changes in the balance sheet
The income statement shows profit, the balance sheet a snapshot
The cash flow statement shows the cash that actually moved

16.quote: Operating takes a look at how well the company generates cash to pay its debt obligations and fund its operating expenses.
16.by: Dr. J, Answers with Dr. J
points: It records cash received from selling products or services
It tracks interest payments and income taxes
It shows whether the core activity produces enough cash alone
It is the most detailed look at how the business runs
